title: An operational failure can become a funding problem before a bank reports losses
summary: A bank can meet its capital and liquidity requirements while remaining exposed to a disruption that reaches customers within hours. Reserve Bank of India Deputy Governor Swaminathan J argued that digital distribution changes the sequence in which stress becomes visible. A failed payment service, an unresolved complaint affecting many customers or the loss of confidence in a platform can precede deposit outflows. By the time a periodic return records a change in the balance sheet, the bank may already be responding to withdrawals. His 9 January address sets out what he expects management and supervisors to demonstrate. It contains no finding that a particular Indian lender was facing a run (pp. 1–3).

Three developments give that sequence systemic significance. Customer acquisition, messages and transfers can all scale quickly, shortening the time available to verify a report and restore confidence. Several institutions may use the same cloud provider, payment rail or data service, so apparently separate lenders can become exposed to one operational failure. Finally, the terms on which digital services operate can damage confidence directly. Poorly disclosed charges, mis-selling, aggressive collection and misuse of customer data create an economic risk even while the underlying loan continues to perform. In the deputy governor’s account, the channel from conduct to liquidity runs through customers’ willingness to continue using the bank. Its strength remains an empirical question (pp. 1–2).

The practical supervisory response starts with how boards rehearse a failure. A documented policy establishes who is nominally responsible. A simulation can show whether authorised decision-makers can restore critical services, communicate under pressure and learn from a near miss. The speaker cited the global IT outage of July 2024 as an illustration of how rapidly disruption at a provider can propagate to sound customers of that provider. Shared infrastructure makes the recovery of a bank dependent on actions outside its own operations. Contracts therefore need to preserve audit and access rights, define incident accountability and support recovery. The regulated entity remains responsible for activities delivered under its name, including through a fintech partner. International providers also create a case for faster supervisory cooperation across borders (pp. 2–3, 5).

Models create another dependency. The speaker identified potential efficiency gains in underwriting, fraud detection, treasury and customer support, alongside difficulties when a vendor embeds a model that the bank cannot explain. An apparently efficient decision can systematically exclude customers through a data proxy. Boards must be able to identify an owner of the outcome and show how unacceptable results are detected and corrected. The intensity of supervision should vary with the institution’s complexity and footprint, while basic governance, data protection and operational controls apply throughout. He proposed testing the activity and the risk involved without committing supervision to a particular technology (pp. 2–4).

The RBI also has to change what it observes. Closer cooperation between on-site and off-site teams, reliable underlying data and supervisory analytics could identify related anomalies earlier. Consumer grievance records are one example of information already generated by the business. A dashboard of case closures says little if the same underlying fault keeps generating complaints. Time to resolution, repeat failures, whether customers received a remedy, and whether the board addressed the source of the problem offer stronger evidence of control quality. The speaker specifically rejected the idea that the absence of complaints is the relevant benchmark for maturity. He also emphasised training, practical simulations and exchanges among supervisors facing similar challenges in the Global South (pp. 4–5).

For a portfolio holding several bank credits, an implication is that diversification by legal issuer can leave a common operational exposure intact. There are two separate empirical tests: whether critical services would fail together, and whether the affected customers could or would move funding once a failure occurred. The speech provides no dependency map, deposit-flow estimate, loss distribution or comparison of bond spreads. Inferring that a particular bank deserves a spread premium would require evidence about both the bank’s exposure and its ability to contain the consequences. The same distinction matters for equity investors: digital expansion may lower distribution costs while increasing the demands on management and on recovery arrangements. No estimate of the net earnings effect or investment recommendation is offered.

questions.question: Do lenders that appear diversified depend on the same service at the point where depositors need access?
questions.detail: A common provider can cause simultaneous disruption, but the address gives no issuer-level map or estimate of substitutability. For bank-credit risk, the important variables include the functions affected, time to switch and whether the fallback relies on the same infrastructure. Seek outsourcing and operational-resilience disclosures, board-level recovery-test summaries and official incident reports. Reconcile claims of multiple suppliers with the practical ability to fail over.

questions.question: How often does customer harm actually precede funding pressure?
questions.detail: The address gives a plausible mechanism, without quantifying the link between complaints, withdrawals and the cost of replacing deposits. The answer would change the weight an investor assigned to complaints as a leading indicator. Compare dated, aggregated service incidents, recurring unresolved grievances and subsequent deposit flows, controlling for ordinary rate-sensitive deposit movements. Bank disclosures and RBI customer-service statistics would be appropriate starting points.

questions.question: What would demonstrate that an institution can challenge decisions produced by its vendors?
questions.detail: Contracts can establish accountability on paper while leaving the bank dependent on an opaque system. That gap matters to the resilience of digital growth and the durability of associated earnings. Ask for evidence from model validation, independent exception reviews, outcomes after customer appeals and vendor-replacement exercises. A separate question for management is whether the board sees repeat failures and remediation costs across business lines.
